concepts.def: Displacement s (vector); velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt = d²s/dt². All are vectors in 2D/3D.
For constant acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ((u+v)/2)t. Useful when a is constant.
Speed is scalar (magnitude of velocity). Velocity is vector — has direction.
If a depends on t: v = ∫a dt; s = ∫v dt. Use calculus rather than SUVAT.
Slope = acceleration; area under graph = displacement. Helpful for visualising motion.
Take a = g = 9.8 m/s² downward (or 9.81). Use SUVAT for projectiles, free fall.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Kinematics — a core area of A-Level Maths.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Kinematics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Kinematics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A particle starts from rest and accelerates at 4 m/s² for 3 seconds. Final velocity is:
options: 12 m/s
7 m/s

mcqs.q: Which SUVAT equation does NOT involve t?
options: v² = u² + 2as
v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²

mcqs.q: How do you use a conversion graph between miles and kilometres?
options: Simple interest grows faster than compound because it has fewer steps.
Pick any point on the line — they're all equivalent.
Find the known value on its axis, draw a line to the graph, then read across (or down) to the other axis.
Look only at the gradient of the line and apply it as a formula.
(-3)^2 equals -9 because the minus is preserved.
Pick any point on the line — they're all equivalent.
(-3)^2 equals -6 because the negative makes you subtract.
9 — squaring a negative gives a positive.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
options: Simple and compound interest give the same total — compound just uses a different formula.
Simple interest grows faster than compound because it has fewer steps.
Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount; compound interest is calculated on the original amount plus accumulated interest.
Pick any point on the line — they're all equivalent.
